newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Seoul stocks hit yr high, interest rates fall.
newsitem.headline: Seoul stocks hit yr high, interest rates fall.

text.p: Hopes for an economic turnaround and sharply declining interest rates fuelled healthy buying of Seoul shares and sent the main stock index soaring to a new 1997 high on Thursday, brokers and analysts said.

The composite stock index shot up 11.25 points to 749.37 in the first few minutes of trading. Profit-taking pulled it off that perch almost immediately, but the index stood at 742.50 at day's end, the highest close so far this year.
Abundant market liquidity pulled down yields on three-year benchmark corporate bonds to 11.86 percent on Thursday after they hit a three-month low of 11.98 percent on Wednesday.
"Falling interest rates mean institutions remain fluid," said Park Key-pyong of Hanyang Securities. "I believe the market is riding a bull-run."
Analysts said the yen's appreciation and rising export prices contributed to raising investor hopes for recovery.

Steve Marvin, head of research at Ssangyong Securities, attributedd the bull-run to "anticipation among investors that the trade account and the economy will start to improve from the second half this year and diminishing fears of a financial meltdown in Korea."
As long as the yen did not depreciate substantially, Asian economic growth remained firm and there were no more major bankruptcies, Marvin said the market would continue to rise.
"I turned bullish in the market at the end of April for those reasons," he said.
Optimistic analysts forecast the market would head for 800 after a consolidation at around 750.
But others disagreed.
"The market will not really turn bullish unless there is firm confidence in an economic recovery and interest rates fall to the 10 percent level," said Choi Bum of C.S. First Boston.
The central Bank of Korea said the current account deficit eased to $1.7 billion in April from $2.36 billion a year ago.
However, economists cautioned against excessive optimism. Slowing imports of capital goods contributed to reducing the deficit, but could bode ill for economic recovery.
"Despite an improvement in April, it is still hard to see an economic recovery," said Lee Choon-yul, economist at Korea Institute of Finance.
Brokers said large-capitalised shares, especially low-priced manufacturers and interest-sensitive construction and financial shares, were in strong demand.
The large-cap sub-index rose 9.83 points, or 1.84 percent, to 1,493.82.

LG Electronics rose 800 won to 14,900 ($16.70), off a new year's high of 15,200 with heavy volume of 1.7 million shares. Brokers said electronic home appliance makers were seen as major beneficiaries of an economic turnaround.
Daewoo Securities traded most actively with 1.74 million shares changing hands. It gained 700 won to 11,200.
"Large-capitalised shares have more room to rise," said Lee Ki-ho, market strategist at LG Securities.
Brokers said active foreign buying, focusing on undervalued blue chips, fuelled the rally. The securities watchdog said net foreign purchase reached 70.3 billion won on Thursday.
Casey Choe of Union Bank of Switzerland said foreign fund managers had tried to expand their Korean investment tools after unloading their holdings since last year.

But Choi of C.S. First Boston said: "Foreign investors have incited the recent rally. But most of them are short-term punters looking for quick profits. They switched from peaked Asian stock markets to Korea."
(Conversion $1 = 892 won)
